Fellow travelers and prospective showgoers, I’d intended to see O, but it was on hiatus, so we booked La Rêve instead. We were staying at Encore, making the theater an easy walk away, and our seats were in about the third row. I knew La Rêve is often compared to—possibly even derivative of—O, so I figured it would be a fair substitute. It may not be O, but it’s a solid substitute.

Maybe La Rêve has a story, but I didn’t understand it, and that wasn’t a problem for me. Before the main performance, a comic lizard-like performer swims in the pool, stays still long enough to resemble a statue, then surprises people in the front rows by sneaking up and spraying them with water.

The main spectacle is the draw: a pool with platforms that rise and lower, performers swimming, diving, and appearing to walk on water, plus a dive from roughly 25 feet above the pool. If you want an impressive major Vegas show without Cirque du Soleil’s very high prices, I recommend La Rêve as a worthy alternative. We left impressed.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching rain through a circular opening of known area. The water is funneled into a measuring tube marked in depth units, such as millimeters or inches. The reading tells how deep the rain would have been if it had fallen evenly over the ground, with no runoff or soaking in.

The opening is often wider than the measuring tube. This concentrates the collected water into a narrower column, making small amounts of rain easier to read accurately. The scale on the tube is adjusted for the difference in area, so the reading still represents actual rainfall depth.

Two common causes of inaccurate readings are poor placement and evaporation. A gauge near trees, buildings, or fences may collect too little or too much because of sheltering or splashing. If the water is not read soon after the storm, some may evaporate.

Marguerite found the book where she always did on Thursdays: wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, as if it had climbed in through the wall. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, a faded library stamp inside the cover. Due date long past.

Eleven Thursdays now. She'd asked the day staff, checked the locks, even stayed late once with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book simply appeared between two and four a.m., and she never caught the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it and a folded square of receipt paper slid out.

*I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*

Marguerite read it twice. Behind her the ovens ticked, and the first trays of rye waited under their cloths.

She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, and wrote on the back: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

The book drop was a milk crate by the back door, and every Thursday around two, Imre found something in it that wasn't milk. First week: *A Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast*, Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, the same book. Third week, the same.

He'd stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the tub of rye starter, its cover gone soft with dough-dusted thumbprints.

Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts, and the book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out near page 112.

He peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right.

*Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? —T.*

Imre looked at the page. Someone had circled nothing; the morel sat there, wrinkled and brown.

He pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over, and wrote *No. Never used one.* Then, after a moment, he added *Come at five, there's bread.* He pressed it back into the book.

In the wicker basket by the back door sat the worn paperback again: *The Borrowers*. For six Thursdays someone had left it here instead of the library two blocks over. A folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her hands on her apron and read: *I can’t get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it’s warm.*

She looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, and tucked the note back into the book. I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.
